turns.answer:
No. The TEAC W-1200 cannot record on Type IV (metal) tapes, and it does not have Dolby noise reduction.

Here's the breakdown:

Feature

	

TEAC W-1200




Record on Type I (normal)

	

Yes




Record on Type II (chrome/high bias)

	

Yes




Record on Type IV (metal)

	

No




Play Type IV (metal)

	

Yes




Dolby B noise reduction

	

No




Dolby C noise reduction

	

No




Dolby S noise reduction

	

No




Other noise reduction

	

Yes, playback-only noise reduction

Its playback noise reduction is not Dolby-compatible encoding or decoding.

TEAC's official specifications confirm these limitations. 
Black – TEAC USA
+1

One important nuance: the W-1200's playback noise reduction is designed to approximate Dolby B decoding, so it can help when listening to older Dolby B recordings.

If your goal is to make high-quality recordings on metal tape with Dolby B/C/S, I would recommend a serviced vintage three-head deck such as the Sony TC-KA7ES or Nakamichi CR-7A instead.

turns.answer:
The TEAC W-1200 has substantially higher wow and flutter than a high-end vintage Nakamichi deck. In fact, transport speed stability is one of the biggest differences between modern cassette decks and the best vintage machines.

Wow and flutter measures short-term variations in tape speed. Lower numbers are better, resulting in more stable piano notes, sustained synthesizer tones, and vocals.

Published specifications, % WRMS

The Nakamichi Dragon's exceptional performance comes partly from its quartz-controlled, dual direct-drive capstan system. Independent historical testing measured just 0.016% WRMS during playback. 
Sound & Vision
+1

Will you hear the difference?

Very likely, especially with sustained piano notes, acoustic guitar, and synthesizers.

At 0.25% WRMS, the TEAC may produce audible pitch instability on demanding material. At approximately 0.02–0.03% WRMS, a properly serviced Nakamichi should sound considerably more stable.

One important caveat: these figures are factory specifications, not measurements of individual machines. A worn Nakamichi with deteriorated pinch rollers or transport problems can perform much worse.

My recommendation: If sound quality is your primary concern, I would choose a professionally restored Nakamichi CR-7A over a new TEAC W-1200. The difference in transport performance is too large to ignore, especially if you intend to make high-quality recordings on metal tape.

turns.prompt: Which one would you pick if you were me?
turns.answer:
I'd pick the Nakamichi CR-7A, provided it's professionally serviced and comes with documented performance measurements.

Based on your questions, you seem to care about three things: recording on metal tapes, Dolby noise reduction, and very low wow and flutter. The CR-7A is significantly better suited to all three than the TEAC W-1200.

Here's how I'd decide:

Priority

	

My pick

Metal tape recording

Dolby B/C noise reduction

Lowest wow and flutter

New equipment and warranty

	

TEAC W-1200




Best balance for your needs

	

Nakamichi CR-7A

I would choose the CR-7A over the Dragon because the CR-7A's recording calibration and manual playback azimuth adjustment make it particularly appealing for serious recording. The Dragon is exceptional for playing tapes recorded on different machines, but its complexity can make restoration expensive.

One condition: I wouldn't buy an unserviced CR-7A just because it has the Nakamichi name. I'd want proof of correct tape speed, wow and flutter, head condition, and recording calibration.

One thing I'm curious about: Are you primarily planning to record new tapes, or play an existing cassette collection? That could change my recommendation considerably.
